This message comes from Google Workspace with Gemini.
One subscription that does it all.
Personalized AI and premium business versions of Gmail, Google Docs, Drive, and more.
Try it free for 14 days at goo.gle/workspace with Gemini.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. A sell-off of AI stocks today dragged
the S&P 500 down 3.7 percent, capping off its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ fell more than five and a quarter percent,
pulling it into negative territory for the year.
Meanwhile, today, President Trump says U.S. tech companies that build
data centers in other countries will face a tremendous tax.
We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country.
We're not going to allow that to happen.
You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else,
and it was very destructive to our country.
It's where we started going behind.
So I just, I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people.
Trump continues to urge Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities
and extract concessions from the developers.
That's even though the midterms ushered in a wave of Democrats
and Republicans pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry data centers.
After a night of intense Russian missile and drone attacks,
residents of Kiev woke to more power and water outages and three damaged bridges.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports many believe Russia is trying
to sever the two banks of the river from each other.
It's chaos and traffic this morning. It's raining.
Standing near one of the bridges across the Nipro River that's temporarily closed,
24-year-old Denis Marchuk said it would be a disaster if the left and right banks were severed.
It would totally affect the life of the city, he says.
People would probably leave their jobs if they worked and lived on opposite sides.
67-year-old Alexander Ivan Karich says the noise last night was terrible.
"You don't get enough sleep and then you can't get to work," he says.
President Vladimir Putin says Russia is retaliating for Ukraine,
damaging the Kerch bridge that links Russia to Crimea.
That bridges a major supply route for Russian forces.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kyiv.
The Department of Energy has officially secured the money it needs to move its staff into the
Department of Education building, as NPR's Janaki Mehta reports.
This is more than just Washington bureaucracy and logistics.
It's also part of the dismantling of the Education Department.
Education Secretary Linda McMahon has spent her tenure doing what she was hired to do,
breaking up her agency. Half the staff were cut last year,
and hundreds of remaining employees have been scattered across Washington.
While the timeline for the actual move isn't clear, the plan to shift
energy department workers into the headquarters of the Ed Department
puts a nail in the coffin, cementing a physical dismantling of the agency.
The historic education building was named for Lyndon B. Johnson,
the former president and school teacher who made education programs,
like helping low-income students, central to his agenda.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News.
Third-party vendors at J.P. Morgan Chase experienced a cyber attack that leaked
personal information of thousands of Chase customers yesterday.
The leaked data includes mostly email addresses and some phone numbers,
but not credit card information.
This is NPR.
A federal appeals court has granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit
that cleared the way for the Army to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa.
The ruling puts in jeopardy the military's plans to deal with dozens of barrels of lead
azide pending further direction by the court.
The Army has said the chemicals are unstable and the risk of explosion is growing,
particularly as temperatures drop.
A new study shows six in ten people who use AI for health advice say they would
believe a chatbot even if it contradicted their health care provider.
NPR's Windsor-Johnson reports.
Talker Research conducted the survey for the virtual care company, MD Live.
Medical director Dr. Maggie Williams says chatbots give quick, confident answers at any hour.
By the time patients come in, she says, many have already asked a chatbot about their symptoms.
That happens every day, multiple times a day, and I think, honestly, many of our patients
have conferred with CLOD or another resource and maybe don't even disclose it.
Williams says the risk goes both ways.
A chatbot could get someone to the ER sooner, but it can also suggest breathing exercises
for chest pressure when someone's having a heart attack.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
Italy's only hedgehog rescue center is overwhelmed with underweight hoglets due to climate change.
Prolonged drought and high temperatures have led to a spike in rescues at the La Nina Center
in Piedmont two years ago.
The center cared for 450 animals, but last year that number rose to over 700.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR News from Washington.
